\chapter{Introduction to Binary Search}
\label{ch:introduction}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced, colback=white, colframe=secondaryblue, boxrule=1pt, arc=2mm]
\textbf{\large\textcolor{primaryblue}{Halve the search space with every comparison --- and prove, with an invariant, that you never lose the answer.}}
\end{tcolorbox}

\chapterfacts{Beginner}{1200}{3}{6}{30}

\begin{plannedbox}[Planned Contents --- this chapter is not written yet]
\textbf{Part A --- Lessons}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*, label=\textbf{A\arabic*.}, itemsep=1pt]
    \item The idea: a sorted array, a guess in the middle, and $\lceil \log_2(n+1) \rceil$ comparisons
    \item The predicate view: every binary search finds the first index where a monotone predicate becomes true
    \item Loop invariants: closed $[lo, hi]$, half-open $[lo, hi)$ and the ``lo is false, hi is true'' form; why loops terminate
    \item Overflow in $mid$, infinite loops, and the off-by-one errors you will make once
    \item Linear search versus binary search; \texttt{std::lower\_bound} and \texttt{std::binary\_search} as the library form
\end{enumerate}
\textbf{Part B --- Patterns} (with the two solved problems of each pattern)
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*, label=\textbf{P\arabic*.}, itemsep=1pt]
    \item \textbf{Classic search in a sorted array} --- Search Insert Position {\small\color{darkgray}(LeetCode 35)}, Guess Number Higher or Lower {\small\color{darkgray}(LeetCode 374)}
    \item \textbf{First true: the predicate view} --- First Bad Version {\small\color{darkgray}(LeetCode 278)}, Find Smallest Letter Greater Than Target {\small\color{darkgray}(LeetCode 744)}
    \item \textbf{Integer roots} --- Sqrt(x) {\small\color{darkgray}(LeetCode 69)}, Valid Perfect Square {\small\color{darkgray}(LeetCode 367)}
\end{enumerate}
\textbf{Connections.} The one-recursive-call view of binary search is the recursion book (Ch 13).
\end{plannedbox}
